pages.name: A ring pulled three ways
pages.task: Two ropes pull on a ring with 3 kN each, 120° apart. What single pull holds the ring still?
pages.why: Lay the two 3 kN pulls nose to tail. The second turns 120° from the first, so they make two sides of a triangle with three equal sides. The side that closes it is also 3 kN, pointing straight down. So a 3 kN pull down holds the ring still.

pages.name: Free the hook
pages.text: Take one part on its own and draw every force on it. That drawing is a [[free-body diagram]]. Each force has a giver. It touches the part, or acts from a distance, as the Earth does. The crane wire pulls the hook up. Each sling leg pulls it down along its own line. The hook stays still, so the three pulls add to nothing. Any leftover force would start it moving. Laid nose to tail, they close a triangle.

pages.name: Forces on the load
pages.task: Now free the load instead. Which forces act on it?
pages.answer: Its weight and the two leg pulls
pages.why: A force on the load needs a giver that touches it, or acts from a distance. The Earth gives its weight. The two legs touch it where they hook on, and each pulls along its own line. The wire touches only the hook. So the load's diagram has three forces, and they close a triangle.

pages.text: As the legs spread, each leg's pull grows. Its vertical part stays at 4.905 kN, half the load, and its sideways part grows. At 60° between the legs, each leg pulls 5.66 kN.

pages.name: Legs at 120°
pages.task: The legs now have 120° between them. What does each leg pull?
pages.why: Each leg is 30° from the horizontal, and sin 30° is 0.5. So each leg pulls 4.905 ÷ 0.5 = 9.81 kN, the whole load. Of that pull, 8.50 kN is sideways. The triangle has three equal sides, just like the ring.

pages.name: The load angle factor
pages.text: Each leg's tension is half the load times one number, 1 ÷ sin θ. That number is the [[load angle factor]]. It is 1.155 at 60° from the horizontal, 1.414 at 45° and 2.000 at 30°. So 60° adds about 15% to each leg's half. Keep each leg well above 30° from the horizontal. A catenary wire pulled taut works the same way. The flatter it hangs, the harder its ends pull.

pages.name: A 2000 kg motor
pages.task: A 2000 kg motor weighs 19.62 kN. It hangs on a two-leg sling, each leg 45° from the horizontal. What does each leg pull?
pages.why: Each leg holds up half the weight, 9.81 kN. At 45° from the horizontal, the load angle factor is 1.414. So each leg pulls 9.81 × 1.414 = 13.87 kN.

pages.name: No weaker, more load
pages.text: Say one leg can safely take 8 kN. A wide angle does not make it weaker. Its strength stays the same while its load grows. At 90° between the legs, each leg carries 6.94 kN, so it is fine. At 120°, the same leg carries 9.81 kN and is overloaded. So the angle alone can overload a sling.

pages.name: Why overloaded?
pages.task: At 120° between the legs, that 8 kN leg is overloaded. Why?
pages.answer: The angle raised the leg's load
pages.why: What the leg can safely take stays 8 kN at any angle. Only its vertical part holds the load up, and that must stay 4.905 kN. Leaning 30° from the horizontal, the leg must pull 9.81 kN to give it. So its load passes its limit.

pages.name: Friction has a giver
pages.text: The push grows to 200 N, and friction grows to match it, so the crate stays still. The deck could give up to 300 N.

pages.name: A crate that stays put
pages.task: The crate weighs 600 N, and μ is 0.5. It stays put under a 150 N push. What friction acts on it?
pages.why: The crate stays still, so the forces along the deck add to nothing. The push is 150 N forward, so friction is 150 N back. μN = 0.5 × 600 = 300 N is only the most the deck could give. Once a crate slides, its grip drops a little below that. Oil or grease lowers μ, so both grips drop.

pages.name: Read the chart right
pages.task: A chart gives the load angle factor by each leg's angle from the horizontal. Your legs each sit 60° from the vertical. Which factor do you read?
pages.why: 60° from the vertical is 90° − 60° = 30° from the horizontal. The factor at 30° is 2.000. So each leg carries the whole load, not 15% more than half.

pages.name: The crane wire
pages.task: With 120° between the legs, each leg pulls 9.81 kN. What does the crane wire pull?
pages.why: Free the hook. Balance works one direction at a time. The sideways parts add to nothing, and so do the up and down parts. Each leg pulls the hook down with a vertical part of 4.905 kN. So the wire pulls up 4.905 + 4.905 = 9.81 kN, just the load.
